title: Hail, Holy Queen
hookLine: the closing prayer calls us poor banished children, sighing in this valley of tears
carry: our life, our sweetness, our hope

cards: Poor banished children of Eve. Mourning and weeping, in this valley of tears. Those lines come from a prayer that monks and nuns sing at the end of the day.
The last service is over, the lights are going down, and they turn toward an image of Mary and sing it slowly, in Latin, before the great silence of the night.
When Catholics finish the five decades of a rosary, they often close with the same prayer. It doesn't pretend life is easy.

teach.b: Salve Regina is Latin for Hail, Queen. It opens like this: "Salve, Regina, mater misericordiae, vita, dulcedo, et spes nostra, salve."

In the traditional English form Catholics say it this way: "Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope. To thee do we cry, poor banished children of Eve; to thee do we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears."
Look at who's speaking. Not the happy and settled. Exiles.

Children of Eve, which means everyone, far from home. The prayer takes the Garden of Eden story seriously: in its picture, people are not where they were made to be. And it doesn't cover the ache with a smile.
Mourning and weeping, it says. Then it turns. It asks Mary, called our advocate, to turn her eyes of mercy toward us, and after this exile, to show us Jesus.
That's the shape: honest about the valley, and hopeful about the way out.
It comes from the monasteries of medieval Europe.

teach.h: OUR LIFE, OUR SWEETNESS AND OUR HOPE.
teach.b: It's often credited to a monk named Hermann of Reichenau, remembered as so disabled he could barely move or speak, and as a writer on music and astronomy anyway.

But the attribution isn't certain, and other names have been suggested. A pious story says Bernard of Clairvaux added the three cries at the end, O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary; that's a legend, not a record.
What's clear is that it traveled: into night prayer in monasteries, and onto the end of the rosary.

how: Catholics often close the rosary with the Salve Regina, and monasteries and religious communities sing it, often in Latin, at night prayer, the last prayer of the day.

a Latin hymn sung at a queen's crowning

games.q: you're writing the prayer that ends the rosary. how do you describe the people praying it?
o: poor banished children, mourning and weeping.
games.why: "poor banished children of Eve... mourning and weeping in this valley of tears." the prayer starts honest, and only then turns to hope.

practice: Think of something that feels like your own valley right now, the thing you'd sigh about if someone asked, and don't tidy it up.

Then, if you pray, say the first line slowly: Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope; if you know the rest, go on. If you don't pray, just notice the order: first the honest sigh, then the hope.

wordCard.voice: Salve Regina. Hail, Queen. The old closing prayer of the rosary and of the monastery night, honest about the valley of tears. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: hail, Queen, mother of mercy. The opening words of the prayer.
